Boyd failed from Liverpool on the 29th December, and the French fleet left Brest, on the 26th of the same month: How then is it possible they should have reached Ireland in 3 days, and the accounts from thence received at Liverpool? Can it be thought that 20,000 French troops, and 17 ships of the line, have surrendered to the inhabitants of Bantry, whose population does not exceed 10,000 souls? It is more natural to think the French have taken that town.—Why were those 20,000 French sent to Dublin, 154 miles from Bantry Bay, and not to Cork, that lies but 9 miles from it? Can it be presumed, that the French fleet, in order to effect a landing at Londonderry, had entered the channel of Ireland so full of dangers, instead of sailing westward, on the main; a route much shorter and less difficult, free from the dangers of the channel, and which would not have exposed them to discovery from Liverpool or Dublin, and meet with every obstacle, that could have frustrated their design. excerpts: Of the intelligence brought by the late arrivals, the most important relates to the French expedition against Ireland. We have collected under this head, every interesting detail we have been able to meet with. By comparing the various accounts, it appears, that the French force when it failed from Brest, consisted of about 50 sail, including transports, of which 17 were of the line, and had on board 25,000 men.—They failed in three divisions, under the command of De Galles, Bouvet and Neuilly; the land troops under the command of general Hoche. They had scarcely left the port when bad weather dispersed them. Chief part of the fleet however rendezvoused at Bantry Bay, but the frigate la Fraternite, on board of which were the commanders of the fleet and land forces, not joining the fleet, after some delay left the Bay, without molestation, except by the wind, and by the best and latest accounts, reached Brest, in divisions without material loss. The expedition appears to have been planned on a large scale. The Toulon fleet which came round to l'Orient, and the armament at Dunkirk were probably to co-operate. Notwithstanding the above failure, the French appear still to have an expedition to Ireland in contemplation.

excerpts: Of the intelligence brought by the late arrivals, the most important relates to the French expedition against Ireland. By comparing the various accounts it appears, that the French failed from Brest with a view of invading Ireland. Their force consisted of about 50 sail, including transports, of which 17 were of the line and about 25,000 men on board. They failed in three divisions, under the command of De Galle, Bouvet and Neilly; the land troops under the orders of Gen. Hoche. They had scarcely left the port when bad weather dispersed them. Chief part of the fleet however, rendezvoused at Bantry Bay, but the frigate la Fraternite, on board of which were the commanders of the fleet and land forces not joining the fleet, after some delay they left the bay without molestation, except from the winds and by the best and latest accounts, reached Brest in divisions, without material loss. The Fraternite was one of the vessels to return. The expedition appears to have caused great alarm in Ireland and England. Had not the elements conspired against the French, little doubt can be entertained but they would have been successful. The expedition appears to have been planned on a large scale. The Toulon fleet which came round to L'Orient, and the armament at Dunkirk were probably to co-operate. The French appear still to have an expedition to Ireland in contemplation. A Paris date of January 29, mentions the arrival of Gen. Hoche in that capital, to give an account of his expedition.

excerpts: BOSTON, OCT. 11. Fraternity.—Capt. Dunbar, from St. Croix, in lat. 23, N. long. 65, 35, W. was boarded by a French privateer brig, from Guadalupe, the capt. of which, with five of his crew, came on board and demanded Capt. D's papers; after examination, ordered his chests and trunks to be opened— took from them all the money and letters— took all the flock cabin stores, spare rigging, sails and blocks—one cask of rum, &c. —suffered his people to steal even knives and forks, spoons, tumblers, and every article remaining in the cabin. The privateer captain put on board us two seamen taken from the brig Favourite, Scituate, of Baltimore, and Mr. Taylor, supercargo, with a cargo of 50,000 dollars. He also wished to get rid of Capt. Scituate and Mr. Taylor, but they insisted on staying aboard the privateer and know the state of their property, which spirited behaviour produced a conduct unworthy a man, for on their refusal to quit the privateer, the capt. indignantly flogged them! Several other American masters and seamen were on board this privateer, among them was Mr. John Barnes, of Marblehead. Before the privateer left us, she took a loop from Rhode-Island, capt. Briggs, bound to Cape-Francois. The captain of the privateer to finish his brutal behaviour, threatened to punish capt. Dunbar—dismissed him with a curse on his country, and a determination to rob every American vessel that could not be made a prize of.

After plundering us of the above articles, he suffered his people to rob us of what they pleased, and so fully devoted were they to the business of thieving, that they took every article they could find, even to the knives, forks, spoons and tumblers, and in fact every article remaining in the cabin.—He then put two seamen on board, that were taken a few days before from the brig Favorite, Sisson, of Baltimore, master, and Mr. Taylor, supercargo, with a cargo of 50,000 dollars. The capt. of the privateer, wished to put capt. Sisson, and Mr. Taylor on board my vessel, but they insisted on staying aboard the privateer, and demanded to know the fate of their property, which spirited behaviour produced on the commander of the privateer, a conduct unworthy a man, for on their refusal to quit the privateer he inhumanly flogged them! Besides capt. Sisson, there were several other American masters and seamen on board the privateer, names, except one, not to be ascertained, this individual's name was John Barnes, of Marblehead:—A few hours previous to our being boarded, the privateer took a sloop from Rhode-Island, capt. Briggs, bound to Cape Francois, who, he said, was a good prize. To add insult to our misfortune this inhuman pirate threatened to take me on board his vessel, and inflict an ignominious punishment on me; and finished his brutal behaviour by dismissing me, with a curse on my country, and a declared determination to rob every American vessel he could not make a prize of.

excerpts: Dreadful SHIPWRECK!! The following account of the shipwreck of the Two Sisters of Rhode-Island, is taken from a Hand-Bill published at BANTRY-BAY, AUG. 12, '97. This morning about 2 o'clock, as some of our fishing boats were working out between the heads, they saw a large ship in the Offing, seemingly in great distress. They stood for the ship, and about 10 o'clock, they boarded her; but there was only one living man on board. She proves to be the Two Sisters, from Rhode-Island, bound for Bristol, and had been out five weeks:—Such a wreck, surely never was seen before! her mizen-mast was all split to pieces, and her main-mast was a stern hanging by some of the wreck; her foremast was also split to pieces, and her fore-top-mast gone by the cap in her steerage or half deck. There were seven men burnt to a coal, and the mate lying under the windlass dead; and as for the Captain, we have no account of him, only the young man found with the wreck says that the Captain and all hands were on deck when some dreadful thunder and lightning came on; and that there were six men on the main-top-sail yard when the mainmast went over the side, and that they were all lost. He says the Captain was on the quarter deck when the mast went, but as he did not see him afterwards, he thinks the wreck hauled him overboard.

excerpts: A melancholy narrative appears in the lists of the disasters of the American ship Two Sisters, of Rhode-Island, bound for Bristol, off Bantry Bay, in August last. On appearance of distress, she was boarded by some people from the land—they found her mizen mast shivered to pieces, her main mast overboard, hanging astern, and her fore topsail gone by the cap—only one living man was found in the wreck, who informed that the ship had been struck by lightning, and that there were six men on the main topsail yard when the mainmast went over the side, all of whom were lost, together with the master of the vessel, who was wanted overboard—seven men were burnt to a coal, and the mate dead; the ship had four feet water in her hold when boarded—was from the Bay of Honduras, with oil, whale bone, logwood and mahogany; the captain's name Gilbert; owner Mr. Mosely of Rhode Island—the people of the coast hauled the vessel up on the beach; the bottom appeared to be in tolerable condition; but masts, spars, sails, &c. worth nothing.

excerpts: January 27. MELANCHOLLY AND DISTRESSING. This morning about a quarter before 6 o'clock, Fire broke out in the lower part of the Dwelling-House of Mr. Andrew Brown, Printer, of this city. The usual spirited exertions of the Citizens prevented the flames from extending to the adjoining houses—and Mr. Brown's Printing Office escaped uninjured. Every humane bosom must be wrung with anguish at the recital of the shocking catastrophe consequent to this event. Mr. Brown, his apprentices, and some other domestics of the family escaped with their lives, by rushing thro' the flames or jumping from the windows—Mr. Brown is very much bruised and is dangerously ill

excerpts: PHILADELPHIA, Jan. 28. Melancholy Event. Never since we have assumed the office of recording passing events to the public, have we entered on the task with more painful sensations, than on the melancholy occasion we have now to mention. About 5 o'clock yesterday morning the house of Mr. ANDREW BROWN, Printer of the Philadelphia Gazette, in this city, was discovered to be on fire. How it originated or progressed, we have not correct information, but the melancholy and almost unparalleled catastrophe, is, we fear, too certain. Mrs. BROWN, two daughters, one son, and a negro boy, have perished in the flames. Two apprentices have suffered severely, and Mr. BROWN is so dreadfully burnt, that but faint hopes of his recovery are entertained.
